At 5:30 p.m. on December 8, 2015, two employees were ascending on a swing-stage
scaffold to inspect the I-beam supporting the scaffold system.  The Company's
Safety Manager asked the employees to ascend on the swing-stage scaffold to
inspect and adjust the I-beam supporting the scaffold system. The Safety Manager
made the request after they attempted to move the swing-stage scaffold from the
ground and one of the I-beam trolleys being used to support the scaffold system
and lifelines became stuck.   The I-beam supporting the swing-stage scaffold was
part of a High Bay Pallet Storage (HBPS) system upper guide rail. The upper
guide rail supporting the swing-stage scaffold was designed to keep the HBPS
system crane plumbed during operation and not designed as a load bearing I-beam.
The upper rail was approximately 76 feet, 9 inches above ground level and
consisted of sixteen I-beam sections. Trolley anchors were used to connect the
Spider swing-stage scaffold system to the I-beam. The upper guide rail I-beam
was connected and supported by cross aisle ties (CATs). It was established
during the investigation, the weight of the scaffold system and the I-beam
exceeded the CAT's maximum intended load capacity. At the time of the accident,
the upper guide rail (I-beam) sections were not connected and had visible gaps
between the rail joints. The Safety Manager and scaffold competent person did
not perform a visual inspection of the upper guide rail prior to using the
scaffold. The rail sections gap increased as a result of the CAT deflection due
to the imposed load. The gaps allowed three (3) I-beam rollers to roll off the
I-beam causing the employee to fall approximately 40 feet to the next lower
level. The employee received multiple internal injuries resulting from a forty
(40) foot fall and being struck by the swing-stage scaffold which also fell from
a height of approximately forty (40) feet, and was killed.  The employee was
fatally injured when a Spider swing-stage scaffold fell approximately 40 feet to
the next lower level. A second employee was left suspended from his lifeline and
suffered minor injuries.

maintenance technician replaced a lid for the test and pushed in the lid. His

amputated. He was hospitalized. The sales manager related that the equipment on
which the employee was injured was made in-house by the firm and still under
development. There were two types of test equipment. One tested the assembly for
the battery lid cover, and the other did the air leak test for the lid cover.

guards in place during the leak test. With the guards in place, the gaps were
0.5 inches (13 mm) on the sides and 0.625 inches (16 mm) on the top. The areas
to the side of the air leak test were covered by a transparent guard, similar to
a face shield. The sales manager said that, though not expecting the employee to
perform another test without the guards, he could have given the employee a tool
or something similar to push the lid to the die, thus avoiding the danger zone.
Replacing the lid to the die by pushing a cart would have kept the employee at a
distance of 21 inches (533 mm).

conveyor system had become jammed. The employee was returning to his workstation

suddenly spin and pinch the employee's left index finger between the axel
trunnion wheel and the wrench. The employee pulled his hand back and realized he
had injured his finger. The employee amputated his fingertip and required
medical treatment without hospitalization.

fourth fingers of the left hand; the end of the ring finger was completely

hospitalization.

At 9:30 a.m. on October 30, 2019, Employee #1, a laborer, was engaged in moving

At 2:00 p.m. on March 14, 2020, an employee was riding on a trailer harvesting

Three employees who worked as Registered Nurses (RN) and two employees who

At 5:45 a.m. on April 18, 2020, Employee # 1, a medical records technician,
contracted COVID-19 and died.
At 12:30 p.m. on April 8, 2020, Employee # 1, a housekeeper, was possibly
cleaning isolation rooms with COVID positive residents. He became ill with
COVID-19 and died.
At 9:50 a.m. on December 5, 2019, an employee was moving a 6-inch diameter,
300-foot-long rubber hose that was connected to a Cornell water pump (Model
B24260-424) being used to direct rainwater towards a drain.  The hose was
kinked, leading to built-up pressure in the hose.  The hose wrapped around the

At 2:48 p.m. on October 3, 2019, an employee was performing work in a
single-family residence and was cutting wood on a table saw when his hand was
pulled into the sawblade. The employee was hospitalized to treat a pinky
amputation.
At 6:00 a.m. on April 14, 2020, Employee # 1, working in transportation
services, suffered exposure to COVID-19 from the community. He became ill with
COVID-19 and died.
At 12:45 p.m. on January 7, 2020, an employee was moving a pile of sheetrock
that was leaning on a wall to another location. The pile of sheetrock pinned his
legs against the wall. The employee dislocated his left knee and was
hospitalized.
At 2:45 p.m. on January 27, 2020, an employee, a service technician, had
returned to the yard and was looking for work until his shift ended. His
supervisor had him get a Sawzall and blades to assist with unpackaging pallets
of tempered glass so the individual sheets could be transferred to A-frames. To
unpackage the glass, employees had to remove part of the outer steel frame,
banding, plywood, and any other packaging so the individual sheets were
accessible. The employee had unpackaged a bundle and the sheets of glass were
standing upright and unsecured when they fell over onto him, pinning him to the
ground. The weight of the glass sheets that pinned the employee was 2,000 lbs or
more, and required a forklift to lift them off him. The employee was
hospitalized to treat a fractured right femur.
At 3:03 p.m. on November 5, 2019, an employee working as a carpenter apprentice
for a residential building contractor was building a parapet on a roof. The
employee was using a 3-foot by 8-foot wooden platform to traverse a staircase.
As the employee crossed the platform, the wood broke causing the employee to
fall through the opening onto the 2nd floor. The employee fractured his spine
and was hospitalized.

An employee, who practices the nursing care of residents, was educating new
employees. The employee had contact with residents  and employees.  The employee
died from non-work related COVID-19 infection at 3:30 p.m. on March 31, 2020.
An employee was working at a general medical and surgical hospital. She worked
as a patient services associate at a state university teaching hospital. She
checked patients in and out, but she had no direct contact with patients. On
March 19, 2020, she left work feeling ill. She had symptoms consistent with an
infection by COVID-19. She never returned to work. At 8:00 a.m. on March 29,
2020, she died. This was an OSHA-covered fatality.
An employee was working at a general medical and surgical hospital. He delivered
supplies throughout the hospital. He was infected with COVID-19. On April 4,
2020, he died. This was an OSHA-covered fatality.
At 5:00 p.m. on December 15, 2019, an employee was working as a maintenance
mechanic for a plastic container manufacturer. They manufacturer recycles used
high density polyethylene (HDPE) containers and produce raw material to produce
new containers. The employee was working on the production floor attempting to
unclog a water ring on a B&B Wash Carousel. He was standing on a step stool
under the equipment to access the water ring. He did not shut the machine down,
do not close the hot water valve and did not lockout the equipment before he
began flushing out the water ring with a water hose. Once the clog was removed,
hot water (approximately 200 degrees Fahrenheit) instantly released and sprayed
the employee. Coworker #1 (supervisor) was not on duty at the time of the
accident. Coworker #2 (production supervisor) came to the assistance to the
employee when nearby coworkers called for help. The employee was taken to a
regional medical center, where he was admitted for more than 24 hours with 3rd
degree burns on multiple body parts.
At 11:00 a.m. on February 19, 2020, an employee and a coworker who worked as
audio and video installation technicians were installing speakers in four
conference rooms. The coworker was the foreman at the job site. The employee
climbed an 8-foot-tall A-frame ladder to install an anchor for a speaker. When
the employee was descending the ladder, he was coming off the 4th step when he
missed a step and fell approximately 4 feet. The employee fell backwards
striking his lower back on the corner of a credenza desk. The employee stated he
had received ladder safety training recently, but he attempted to climb down the
ladder holding a screwdriver and a crimping tool in his hands. He claimed to
have maintained 3 points of contact with the ladder. The employee fractured his
vertebrae and ribs and was hospitalized for one day.
At 9:30 a.m. on October 11, 2019, an employee working as a technician for a
power and communication line installation company was attempting to lift a
manhole cover. The cover slipped and landed on the employee's left hand. The
employee partially amputated his middle finger, requiring medical treatment
without hospitalization.
At approximately 12:45 p.m. on April 4, 2020, an employee was spraying the floor
with a water hose and removing floor drain covers to empty drain traps and spray
out floor drains. The employee attempted to remove a section of a floor drain
cover on which was resting one leg of a Translicer 2000 food slicing machine.
When the cover would not come out, the employee attempted unsuccessfully to move
the machine. The employee then tried again to remove the drain cover. The
machine leg/caster dropped into the drain when the cover was removed. The
machine tipped over and fell on the employee, pinning the employee to the floor
and killing the employee.
At 2:00 p.m. on April 4, 2020, an employee was working as a civilian for a
branch of the armed forces of the United States. This branch guarded the coast
of the United States. He was a machinist. He was operating a metal shear. He
placed his left index finger in the point of operation. His left index finger
was amputated all the way to the first knuckle. The narrative did not specify
whether this was the distal or the proximal knuckle. Possibly the amputation was
limited to the fingertip. The employee was treated without hospitalization. The
employer did not report the amputation to OSHA until 10:30 a.m. on April 6,
2020. The report came in via a telephone call.
At 12:00 a.m. on November 5, 2019, an employee was working in a nine foot deep
trench installing pipe. While working, the trench walls collapsed onto the
employee and he was buried under the soil. The employee was killed by the
combined injuries due to blunt force trauma to the head and torso and
asphyxiation.
At 2:30 p.m. on January 17, 2020, an employee was operating a 60-volt DeWalt
DCS577 Cordless Worm Drive with a 7 ? inch radial blade to cut a piece of 1/8
inch Masonite that was 4 feet by 11 inches wide that had been placed atop of two
trash cans for support. While cutting, the Masonite shifted, and the employee
reached with her left hand to stabilize the Masonite.  The employee's left ring
finger was severely lacerated, and the pad of her thumb was degloved.  The
employee was treated without hospitalization.
At 9:06 a.m. on February 22, 2020, an employee, a veterinary assistant in a
veterinary pet hospital, was attempting to draw blood from a cat when the animal
became agitated and bit her. The employee was restraining cat in a "scruff hold"
while a coworker, another veterinary assistant, attempted to insert the needle
to take the sample. The initial attempt was not successful so the workers
decided to trade places so that the employee could draw the sample. As they
prepared to change places, the animal suddenly became agitated and twisted in
the employee's grip and bit her on the right middle finger. The employee was
immediately given first aid for the bite and sent to an occupational health
clinic for evaluation. The employee was evaluated and given oral antibiotics and
ibuprofen and sent home. The following morning the condition of the wound had
worsened and the employee went to the emergency room and was admitted for
treatment with IV antibiotics and remained in the hospital for approximately
four days.
At 8:30 p.m. on March 27, 2020, Employee #1, a machine operator, was using a
utility knife to cut a mat that had become jammed in the drive roller at the end
of the D-Oven machine. Employee # 1 slipped and grabbed the material in order to
stop himself from falling. His left hand and forearm were pulled between the
drive roller and the free-rolling conveyor system. Employee # 1 suffered a
fractured left ulna. He was hospitalized.
At 7:50 p.m. on February 7, 2020, an employee was dumping trash into a dumpster
using a Unicarriers forklift and was standing on the edge rail on top of the
dumpster to push the trash into the container. The employee started descending
using the forklift's mast when he fell to the ground. Coworkers heard a noise
and went to see what it was and found the employee on the ground by the forklift
in a pool of blood. The employee was rushed to the hospital to treat a traumatic
brain injury and was in a comma for more than a week.
At 2:30 p.m. on November 26, 2019, an employee had just added oil to a Hurricane
300 Industrial Vacuum, which was being used to remove spent abrasive from a
pipe.  The employee was a painter and machine operator who worked directly for
the employer.  This vacuum is configured on a trailer to allow for
transportation. The employee had climbed on the frame of the trailer part of the
vacuum to gain access to the oil port. After he finished adding oil, the worker
had replaced the access plate and was tightening and securing the wing screw. At
that point, the employee either slipped or stepped off the trailer and the ring
on his right ring finger caught on the wing screw that he was tightening.  The
employee continued to go to the ground, with his ring caught on the wing screw.
The employee sustained an amputation of his right ring finger. Initially, the
employee was treated at Los Banos Memorial Hospital in Los Banos but was later
transferred to UC Davis Medical Center in Sacramento.  The employee was treated
without hospitalization. Although the employer is being cited for a violation,
it was not considered accident-related. The object that directly harmed the
employee was the employee's ring being caught on the wing screw, and the
employee's body weight continuing to the ground, while the ring stayed caught on
the screw.
At 8:45 am, on April 6, 2020, Employee # 1 was working for a framing contractor.
Employee # 1 was supervising a framing operation on the second level when he
got too close to the edge and fell12 feet to the ground.  Employee # 1 suffered
unspecified fractures and was hospitalized.
At 2:35 p.m. on March 24, 2020, Employee #1 was feeding 126-inch long by
1.315-inch diameter steel stock tubing into a Tauring Group DS 60CN Plus
Pyramidal bending machine (#10001517). Employee #1 controlled the feed by means
of a foot actuated control. As the second piece of stock tubing was fed into the

At 9:45 a.m. on February 12, 2020, an employee was labeling tires that were on a

At 11:45 a.m. on September 16, 2019, an employee was using a table saw, taking

sawblade.  The employee's fingers were amputated, resulting in hospitalization.
At 2:00 p.m. on March 6, 2020, an employee was working at an automotive body
shop. It was one outlet of a nationwide chain of auto body shops. The employee
was an auto body technician. He was straightening the rear body panel of a
vehicle being repaired. He was using a chisel and hammer. When he struck the
hammer against the chisel, a small piece of metal was chipped off the chisel. It
landed in the employee's eye. The employee was wearing safety glasses at the
time, but the metal fragment found its way past the glasses. The employee was
hospitalized. The employer did not contact OSHA within 24 hours of the
work-related injury that resulted in an inpatient hospitalization. The manager
at the facility stated that the incident occurred on a Friday and that he did
not find out until Saturday that the injured employee had been hospitalized.
Company policy was to report incidents to the corporate office, which would then
contact OSHA. The manager stated that he did not submit the information to
corporate until Monday, as the offices were closed on the weekend. Corporate did
not contact OSHA until the following Thursday, March 12, 2020.
At 10:01 a.m. on February 27, 2020, an employee working as a millwright at a

investigate a suspected maintenance issue when a coworker, the stacker operator,
released a wood package striking the employee's leg. The employee fractured his
right tibia and fibula and sustained abrasions, requiring hospitalization.
At 1:15 p.m. on March 18, 2020, Employee #1 and a coworker, employed by a
roofing company, were engaged in roofing activity at a commercial construction
site.  As the coworker held a ladder at its base, Employee #1 climbed the ladder

cord, the cord snapped, causing Employee #1 to fall.  He fell a height of 30
feet and struck the pavement. Employee #1 sustained traumatic head injuries and
was killed.
At 9:00 a.m. on March 18, 2020, an employee operating/loading and unloading
metal parts from a hydraulic press. Press dies closed while the employee was
loading and unloading parts.  The employee was killed after being crushed by

At 8:50 a.m. on October 17, 2019, an employee who worked in a warehousing and

forklift. The employee sustained internal injuries and was hospitalized.
At 11:00 a.m. on March 16, 2020, Employee #1, employed by a plumbing and heating

At 4:50 p.m. on March 6, 2020, an employee was working at a full-service
restaurant. It appears that he was a cook or kitchen worker, but not the lead

employee walked into the cooking area, grabbed the freezer door to open it, and

treated without hospitalization.
At 3:30 p.m. on November 8, 2019, an employee working as an operating engineer
for a property leasing company was installing a new electrical outlet in an
apartment vanity room. The employee had cut two sides of a piece of plywood with

cut the power. The employee sustained a deep laceration to his right forearm and

and received additional surgery in another hospital.
At 10:30 a.m. on March 18, 2020, Employee #1 entered a grain bin to break corn
loose after a break. The employer had not seen Employee #1 in a while, so he and
a coworker went looking for Employee # 1. Employee # 1 was killed by
asphyxiation when he was engulfed by grain. Employee #1's body was recovered at
approximately 4:00 p.m. by first responders.
At approximately 4:37 p.m on March 18, 2020, Employee # 1 was in a tree,
trimming the tops of trees at a private residence. He was using a pole saw,
approximately 9 feet 6 inches long, without insulation, while working within 10
feet of energized power lines. He was holding the pole with both hands. The back
of the tree was about 7 feet 6 inches from the power lines and the front was
approximately 4 feet 2 inches of the 21,000 volt power lines. Employee # 1 made
contact with the power lines, was electrocuted, causing him to catch on fire for
almost an hour before the power could be shut off and fire department could
retrieve him. He was killed. He died of cardiac arrest primarily and secondarily
of burning to death internally. Employee # 2, the supervisor/sales rep, was
responsible for setting crews up for jobs, look for site specific hazards and
address those hazards in a safety meeting prior to work starting. He did not do
that, nor did he ensure the power was shut off prior to work starting.  The fire
department notified the district office at approximately 6:00 p.m. and the CSHO
arrived on the scene at approximately 7:00 p.m., the same day while Employee # 1
was still onsite. Employee # 1 was still in the position that EMS left him after
they tried to revive him. He was laying supine, with electrical burn marks on
both hands.
At 1:30 p.m. on February 7, 2020, an employee, a mechanic, was flushing the
coolant system and looking for an oil leak beneath a 2008 BMW 135i.  The
employee elevated the car on a lift, removed the hose to the radiator and
drained the coolant. The employee then replaced the hose, lowered the car,
filled the radiator with new coolant and water, and turned the engine on.  The
employee then elevated the car again to look for oil leaks beneath. After
approximately five minutes, the coolant hose beneath the car disconnected and
hot coolant and water splashed all over the employee. The employee suffered
first degree burns on the left side of his face, right upper arm, left front and
back upper torso and left ankle and was hospitalized in a medical burn unit for
five days.

At 12:00 noon on September 17, 2019, an employee was using a punch press and was
removing a product when the machine cycled and her finger was caught between the
die. The employee suffered an amputation to her left ring finger and was treated
without hospitalization.
At 12:35 p.m. on November 5, 2019, an employee who worked as a Fire Fighter for
a city fire department was attempting to rescue a victim trapped inside of a
trench collapse. The employee was in the trench when an additional collapse
occurred causing stone and soil land on top of him. The employee fractured his
ribs, broke an ankle and sustained a medial collateral ligament Injury (MCL) to
a knee, requiring hospitalization.
At approximately 12:00 a.m. on April 7, 2020, an employee was operating the Prab
Vertical Axis Crusher processing zirconium turnings when he was overcome by what
was described as a flash fire. His coworkers working near the area were able to
evacuate without injury.  The employee died in the fire.
At approximately 12:16 p.m. on April 8, 2020, an employee was pinned between a
sprocket. The employee was hospitalized to treat an amputation of his right
index fingertip.
At 6:50 a.m. on October 10, 2019, an employee was cutting pants on an Eastman
Machine Textile cutting machine. The employee had her left middle finger in the
path of the cutting blade when the cutter came forward. It is unknown if the
employee manually moved the cutter forward or if after making the cut, the
employee pushed the cutter back and it hit the backstop and rebounded forward.
The tip of the employee's left middle finger was amputated and was treated
without hospitalization.
At 8:15 a.m. on October 14, 2019, an employee, a maintenance worker, was
troubleshooting a rubbing sound in a screw conveyor when he contacted the auger
and his left arm was pulled in to the conveyor. The employee was hospitalized to
treat a left hand amputation.
At 11:00 a.m. on October 3, 2019, an employee was working for a firm that
processed and sold, at wholesale, fish and seafood. She was feeding fish into a
Baader model 417 fish head cutter. Fish were caught on pin chains and fed the
fish into the cutter. The machine was 48 in high (1.22 m high) where the fish
were taken up by the chains. The fish were fed vertically. There was a 4 in by 3
in (102 mm by 76 mm) finger guard. There was a 10 in high (254 mm high) opening
from the top of the fish guide. There was a 5.5 in (140 mm) space blow the
finger guard. It was 7.5 in wide (191 mm wide) at the guide area. There was a
distance of 3 in (76 mm) from the bottom warning sign to the guide. The height
of the warning sign area was 7 in (178 mm). There were two slanted saws and a
splitter bar. The finger guard moved from the seven o'clock to the nine o'clock
position. It bent backward 60 degrees. The employee was feeding fish into the
machine, when a cutting blade amputated one of her fingertips. The employee was
treated without hospitalization. In a later interview, she said that feeding the
fish to the machine was not her regular job. She also said that she had not been
trained to feed the fish into the machine. She said that she did not know how
she had contacted a cutting blade. She says she was not reaching for a fish head
stuck on a cutting blade. The injured worker's incident report says that she had
reached in too far when she fed the fish in. It was suspected that a fish head
had become caught on the cutting blades and that the worker had reached in to
remove it from the saw blades. One operator had seen the employee reach into the
machine ten to fifteen times. That operator stated that there was a stick for
freeing a stuck fish head. The machine's manufacturer was attempting to design a
new guard for the machine or to install a light curtain.
At 3:00 p.m. on October 9, 2019, an employee who worked for a mineral wool
manufacturer was threading an L9 Chain Former on a laminating machine when his
fingers became caught in the running nip point between two running rollers. The
employee lacerated and crushed his fingers and required medical treatment but
was not hospitalized.
At 7:45 a.m. on October 14, 2019, an employee was attempting to wedge a fifth
wheel off of a truck trailer with a crowbar when the trailer shifted, pinching
his abdomen.  The employee suffered a heart attack and died.
At 8:00 a.m. on August 2, 2019, Employee #1, employed by a construction company,
was unloading caging materials on the fourth floor of a new commercial building,
a multiemployer construction project.  As he lifted a boxed pallet of materials
from the forks of an aerial lift to a receiving platform, the load shifted.
Both Employee #1 and the load fell to the concrete surface, a fall height of 32
feet.  The pallet fell on top of Employee #1 and crushed his head, chest, and
abdomen.  Employee #1 was killed.
At 11:15 a.m. on October 17, 2019, an employee was removing the bolts from a
control motor operator valve in the coker unit of an oil refinery when there was
a steam release. The employee was hospitalized to treat burns on his back.
At 10:30 a.m. on October 15, 2019, an employee working for a construction
machinery manufacturer was operating an overhead crane to move a steel I-Beam
from the "drop" area of the Pre-Fabrication Department (Department 50). The
employee was moving the I-Beam to an area were the beams would be picked up as
scrap by a local metal recycling company. As the employee was lifting the beam,
it struck the conveyer and kicked out impacting the stack of neighboring beams
that were stacked three high. The flange of the beam got caught on the flange of
the middle and/or top beam in the stack that was located between the employee
and the beam.  The employee recognized that the beam had been struck and made an
attempt to stop the top beam from falling with his left hand as he was holding
the overhead crane controller in his right hand. The employee then used his
right hand and stepped forward with his left leg.  The beam fell 27-1/2-inches
from the top of the stack to the ground onto employee's left leg. The employee
fractures his tibia and fibia and was hospitalized.
At 10:30 a.m. on May 25, 2019, an employee was cleaning the rust off of the
control station for the stabilizers of a catering lift truck. The employee
cleaned the rust off of the control station for the stabilizers and the
stabilizers came down to the ground. The employee was testing the van body by
lifting it from the driver's cabin control station when a food cart got stuck
between the van body and the platform. The food cart began raising the platform,
instead of it being raised by the van body. The employee grabbed a bar, went
underneath the platform, and pushed the cart out causing the platform to go into
a free fall. The platform crashed onto the employee's body and pinned him to the
top of the driver's cabin. The employee was hospitalized to treat a fractured
collarbone and a ruptured artery.
At 2:39 p.m. on October 1, 2019, an employee was sitting on the floor
troubleshooting a defective air clamp when a coworker turned on the pneumatic
the moving blades and suffered an amputation to his right middle finger. The
employee was treated without hospitalization.
At 6:00 p.m. on October 17, 2019, an employee who was supplied by a staffing

At 11:15 a.m. on October 30, 2019, an employee was working as a production
supervisor at a brewery. The employer was changing hoses on a metal tank that
was 7 feet (2.1 meters) tall and 42 inches (1.07 meters) in diameter. In the
tank, wort, the liquid extracted from the mashing process, was boiling at
approximately 212 degrees F (100 degrees C). Hops were added to the mixture,
followed by a whirlpooling of the mixture to bring the hops to the middle. The
employee was about to change hoses to move the brew liquid using a hose and a
pump. The boil kettle had metal piping attached to the vessel. The first
pipeline attachment on the tank was the reducer clamp, followed by a butterfly
valve and a hose clamp. They were all in a straight line, with the hose clamp
having an open/close valve handle. As the employee was unclamping the hose clamp
to change the hose attachment, he inadvertently removed the butterfly valve,
releasing the boiling wort. The employee was wearing shorts and steel toe hiking
boots. The hot liquid poured onto his shin and into his work boots. The employee
suffered second-degree scald burns to his left ankle (exposed Achilles) and
foot. The burns covered 2.5 percent of his total body surface area (TBSA). He
was hospitalized. He was first seen at an emergency room and then had a referral
to a burn center the next day at a different hospital. The owner of the company
was not onsite. The employer reported the incident to DOSH by phone at 4:30 p.m.
on the following day, complying with the reporting requirements. DOSH arrived at
the site at 2:45 p.m. on November 13, 2019. Contributing factors were that the
employee did not have proper PPE for an unforeseen release of thermally
hazardous liquids, and that the hot liquid or pressure was not relieved from the
piping before the piping attachment was dismantled or changed. One SAR was
issued for 3329(d) and a Serious was issued for 3302(b). Two Generals were
issued for 5194(e)(1) and 5194(h)(2).

At 11:15 a.m. on December 19, 2019, two employees were replacing fluorescent
lighting ballasts in the conference room's overhead lighting system. The circuit
breaker labeled "Lighting" (circuit #3 in panel H-B) was opened, and Employee #1
used a Fluke Model 324 meter to verify that the power supply wire feeding one of
the fluorescent ballasts in the lighting fixtures was deenergized. He did not
verify that the other power supply wires present in the fixtures were
deenergized, or that the neutral wire did not have any voltage or current
present. Employee #1 began removing the fluorescent ballast from the fixture by
cutting the power supply wire and stripping the insulation from the wire to
insert it into a wire connector. He then cut the neutral wire from the ballast
and, while attempting to strip the insulation from the conductor still connected
to the wiring system, he received an electric shock which caused his body to
"torque," causing him to lose his balance and fall approximately 5 feet from the
portable A frame ladder he was standing on to the floor surface of the
conference room. Employee #1 suffered a fractured humerus in his left arm and
was hospitalized.   CalOSHA identified several causal factors, including but not
limited to: -The employee (authorized person) failed to lock the disconnecting
means in the "open" position on all electrical branch circuits providing power
to a 277v lightning system with a shared neutral conductor. -The employee did
not properly test the conductors in the light fixture that he was working on to
verify that no voltage was present. -The employer failed to identify and correct
the hazardous condition of employees performing work on electrical systems with
shared neutral conductors. -The employees had not received training on
identifying and deenergizing electrical systems which utilize multiple line
voltage conductors sharing a common neutral conductor.

At 5:45 p.m. on December 10, 2019, an employee was working as a salesclerk or

approximately 30 lbs (13.6 kg.). The store supervisor was standing on the ground
less than 10 feet (3.0 meters) away. The employee was using a Werner 10-foot
(3.0-meter) aluminum A-frame ladder with retractable coasters to reach the box.
She carried the box down and rested it on the second shelf level. As she lifted
the box and was descending the ladder again, one of the carrying holes in the
sides of the box in which her hands were inserted began to slip. This happened
as she was stepping down with her left foot. She lost her balance and landed
awkwardly on the polished concrete floor. She suffered broken bones and
fractures in her left ankle. She was transported to a teaching hospital
associated with a university's medical school. She was hospitalized for more
than two days. The store manager notified DOSH of the accident at 12:35 p.m. on
the following day. A safety and health inspection officer arrived at the
location at 2:30 p.m. on December 31, 2019, and met with the store manager to
open the investigation. The employee's unawareness of her body position and work
environment, such as her elevation with reference to the ground level,
contributed to her foot injury as she was descending the A-frame ladder. Also,
she did not maintain three-point contact as she was carrying the large box down
the stepladder.

knot bound up. He tried to free it by bouncing on the line, and as he did so,
the line slipped off the stub nut and slipped down the trunk to the ground. The
employee fell 30 feet to the grass.  The employee fractured his right fibula and
dislocated his elbow. He was treated in a local hospital for seven days
following the fall. The employer has since required that no rappelling is
allowed, and climbers must be secured to both the climbing line and their
lanyard until they are back on the ground.
On May 6, 2020, at approximately 6:24 a.m., the employer was harvesting lettuce
in the field.  The employer had called out the mechanic to repair the harvesting
machines in the agricultural field.  The employee was struck and run over by a
backing company vehicle in the field/road area.   At the time of the
investigation, the scene has been changing and the vehicle moves to the main
office/yard.  A coworker was backing up a Dodge Ram 4500 truck on the dirt road,
and struck and ran over an employee walking/working in the field/road.  The
coworker felt a bump, but thought it was a hole.  The employee died of multiple
blunt force injuries after backing the vehicle.
At 9:00 a.m. on May 5, 2020, Employee # 1 was found unresponsive at his home. He
died of COVID-19 disease.
On April 25, 2020, Employee # 1 was at home feeling ill and called in sick with
staging the last two pallets for that line when he placed the two pallets down
and then attempted to get the top pallet with the forks to place it in front of
the other one. The coworker did not set the forks well and he hit the pallet
the fence on an angle while a coworker supported the sash. The employee was in
the process of finishing the sash when he turned to grab another sash. While
turning to grab the other sash, the employee contacted the cutting tool with his
left hand causing his hand to be sucked into the machine. The employee amputated
his pinky and ring fingers and amputated half of his middle and index fingers.
The employee required medical treatment without hospitalization.
At 12:30 p.m. on November 21, 2019, an employee was rigging a shoring pipe.  The
rigging equipment caught the wedge that held the pipe in place.  The pipe moved
and pinned the employee against the shoring wall.  The employee sustained a
fractured pelvis and wrists and was hospitalized.
At 9:30 a.m. on April 17, 2020, Employee # 1 was cleaning/disinfecting patient
rooms. He had a possible exposure to SARS CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19
related illnesses. He had health complications related to COVID 19 and died.
At 3:00 a.m. on February 1, 2020, Employee #1 (sanitation worker) was in the
process of cleaning a lettuce line incline conveyor by using a pressure washer
nozzle. Employee #1 turned off the equipment prior to performing the task by
turning off the control switch located in close proximity to the lettuce line
incline conveyor operator. Employee #1 was standing on a small platform, where
the operator normally stands, in front of the conveyor, then noticed a piece of
lettuce stuck in the conveyor belt and attempted to retrieve it using his left
hand. Employee #1 accidentally activated the conveyor belt, when his body
pressed on the control switch, lodging his left arm between the conveyor belt
and the drive pulley. Employee #1 suffered bone fractures to his left arm and
fingers and was hospitalized.
At 2:35 p.m. on October 18, 2019, an employee was cleaning a restroom when a
plastic emergency exit sign fell and hit her in the eye and face. The employee
was hospitalized to treat a laceration to her eye.
At 1:30 p.m. on February 10, 2020, an employee was working as a delivery truck
driver picking up donated grocery items from various locations. The employee was
working by himself in the rear loading dock area of a grocery store and was
loading donated food items into the back of the box truck. While standing on the
elevated dock's edge, the employee attempted to pull the strap attached to the
rear roll-up door handle. As the door was pulled down, the employee's left hand
extended out in attempt to brace his position. One of the horizontal slats on
the sliding door caught the employee's gloved left hand, amputating the tips of
his middle and ring fingers. The employee also suffered nerve damage and loss of
sensation to the tips of his fingers.  The employee was hospitalized for
treatment.
At 11:00 a.m. on April 20, 2020, an employee reached into a sand mixer chute
with his hand.  The blade from the horizontal auger caught two of his fingers,
resulting in an amputation. The employee was hospitalized.
At approximately 10:00 A.M. on April 15, 2020, an employee, working for a
heating and air conditioning contractor, was climbing a ladder to the roof. The
ladder slipped out and employee fell approximately 10 feet. The employee was
hospitalized and treated for a broken ankle.
At 10:30 p.m. on March 10, 2020, an employee was operating a Greenworks
2,000-psi electric pressure washer. The employee was pressure washing the inside
lobby area of the restaurant and dining area. The employee was using water mixed
with Q5R Heavy Duty Degreaser. The hose of this pressure washer was 8-feet in
length and was pressurized to approximately 2,000-psi. It was determined through
interviews and after reviewing the security footage that the employee was trying
to un-kink the high-pressure hose. The employee stated that the hose kept
kinking up on him, causing the pressure washer to cut off and lose pressure. The
employee stated that he reached with his left hand to grab the high-pressure
hose. When attempting to un-kink the high-pressure hose, the hose had busted in
his hand. The employee sustained a laceration on his left hand, in the webbing
in between his left middle and index finger. The penetrating water had
penetrated to his upper palm and almost to his wrist. The employee also
sustained nerve damage and contusions. The employee was hospitalized.
On April 14th or 15th, 2020, Employee #1, a maintenance mechanic, began to
experience symptoms associated with COVID-19. He tested positive for COVID-19 on
April 17, 2020. On April 20, 2020 at approximately 3:30p.m. to 4:00 p.m.,
Employee #1 started to experience shortness of breath and went to the hospital.
He died shortly after. It is possible that Employee #1 suffered from
pre-existing respiratory conditions.
At 12:00 a.m. on April 3, 2020, Employee # 1 died after providing care for
patients. She came in contact with a COVID-19 infected patient. Employee # 1
became infected with the COVID-19 virus and had complications.
At 1:59 p.m. on October 25, 2019, an employee was setting up materials in
preparation for installing glass at a commercial facility. The employee was
diagnosed with valley fever after working at the site and was hospitalized.
At 10:00 a.m. on February 3, 2020, an employee working as a molding machine
operator for a plastics manufacturer was moving a metal plate. The plate moved
trapping the employee's finger between the plate and the workstation table. The
employee amputated his right middle fingertip and was hospitalized.
At 7:00 a.m. on April 15, 2020, an employee working for a meat packing company
was checking the alignment of a conveyor system for the bacon line. The employee
placed his hand on the edge of the conveyor system to support himself. The
rotating rollers were not being properly guarded. As he looked under the
machine, the employee caught his left hand between the conveyor belt and a pinch
point. The employee amputated his left thumb and required hospitalization.
At 4:00 a.m. on April 9, 2020, an employee working as a supervisor for a metal
tubing and conduit manufacturer was troubleshooting the tape dispenser of a 3
Mill Deburrer machine. The employee was working with a coworker (a finishing
technician) to troubleshoot the machine. When the employee placed his hand in
the jaw of the tape dispenser, the machine unexpectedly started catching his
left index finger. The employee amputated the fingertip and required medical
treatment without hospitalization.
At 4:30 a.m. on April 8, 2020, an employee was working for a firm that made
frozen specialty foods. He worked in machinery maintenance. He was performing an
annual preventative maintenance task. He was replacing a grade-80 chain on a
V-Mag lift machine. The employee was positioned on a ladder stand. He was going
to remove the chain from overhead. He had removed the bottom pin holding the
chain, but he failed to remove the top pin connecting the chain to its cradle.
The cradle was not clamped per instructions. The extra weight created a lot of
resistance, but the employee continued to pull. With his right hand, he lifted
the chain to release its tension. With his left hand, he rolled the chain off a
sprocket. He was able to raise the chain and cradle high enough to get his
fingers between the chain and sprocket. The chain slipped out of his grasp, and
his left hand became caught between the sprocket and the chain. The chain and
cradle fell, creating a pinch point between the chain and the sprocket. He
suffered a fracture to his left middle finger and the amputation of the tip of
his left little finger. He was treated without hospitalization. He had locked
out the equipment, but he did not follow written work order procedures for this
annual preventative maintenance.
At 1:30 p.m. on April 10, 2020, an employee working for a farmers cooperative
was assisting a coworker with connecting a Chevrolet 2500 HD Truck to a dual
tank anhydrous ammonia trailer located in a field of bean stubble. The employee
was holding the tongue of the trailer up while the coworker was backing up the
truck. When the coworker started to back-up the truck, the rear wheels started
spinning. The coworker accelerated the truck to assist in gaining some traction.
When the spinning wheels came into contact with dry ground, the truck lurched
back. The employee became caught between the truck and the tank trailer. The
employee sustained crushing injuries to his pelvis and was hospitalized.
At 5:15 a.m. on March 21, 2020, an employee was walking toward the service deli.
She was not wearing slip-resistant shoes, and she slipped on the wet floor and
fell.  The employee sustained a back injury, requiring fusion surgery. The
employee was hospitalized.
At 7:30 p.m. on November 9, 2019, an employee was working as a bread associate
in a commercial bakery and was cleaning a Sinmag SM-307 dough moulder by hand
when her hand got caught in the in-running rollers of the machine.
Lockout/tagout was not executed prior to cleaning operations and the hopper did
not extend high enough to prevent the employee from coming into contact with the
in-running rollers. The employee suffered a partial left thumb amputation and
was transported to a local medical center by her supervisor for medical
treatment to include surgery.
At 7:15 a.m. on April 23, 2020, an employee was working for a manufacturer of
brick and structural clay tile. Among the firm's products was pavers. Pavers had
to be banded for shipment. Two machines were required. There was a machine to
band horizontally and another machine to band vertically. One machine, a Signode
large pallet traveling on a conveyor and a positioning table.  The employee
sustained crushing injuries and died from his injuries while receiving treatment
at a local hospital.
At 3:15 a.m. on December 31, 2019, a semi-truck was traveling north bound on I-5
from Kingsford California, when the trainee truck driver reportedly fell asleep
while driving.  The truck left the roadway into the center median and turned
over onto its side.  The trainee and trainer sustained serious injuries and were
admitted to Asante Medical Center for medical treatment and an overnight stay.
At 1:30 p.m. on November 6, 2019, an employee was flagging to control traffic
when she was struck by a vehicle. The employee was hospitalized to treat
multiple injuries.
An employee was working as a receptionist at a nursing care or skilled nursing
facility. She felt sick at home and went to the hospital. She suffered from
complications after exposure to COVID-19. At 3:00 p.m. on April 8, 2020, she
died. This was an OSHA-covered fatality.
At approximately 10:35 a.m. on April 8, 2020, an employee was driving a sprayer
cart on a golf course. The employee drove the cart horizontally across a 27
degree sloped hillside.  The cart then rolled down the hill and pinned the
employee underneath.  The employee was killed by blunt force trauma and internal
bleeding.
At 10:45 p.m. on April 9, 2020, an employee was cleaning a saw approximately 10
feet away from the front loader that was used to bring and hoist a palm tree to
be planted. A 24-foot palm tree that was strapped to a front loader boom became
unhooked from the boom, striking the employee. The employee was killed.
An employee, a psychiatric care physician at a general medical and surgical
hospital, provided patient care at the hospital.  He died after contracting
COVID-19 on April 6, 2020.  The time,  date, and other details of the events
leading to exposure were not supplied in the narrative.
At approximately 2:20 p.m. on April 9, 2020, an employee was sweeping dust and
manure around a pit that housed the manure transfer conveyor system. The
employee was cleaning around a pit that housed a manure transfer conveyor
system.  The employee fell over a guardrail system and onto the conveyor system.
The employee was then dragged over 100 feet where the employee  was crushed by
the conveyor's paddles at a manure transfer station. The employee was killed
after suffering several blunt injuries to the body and the head.
At 9:30 a.m. on February 24, 2020, an employee was walking with paper in his
hand when he stepped into the warehouse aisle and was struck by an oncoming
forklift. The employee was hospitalized to treat a fractured arm.
At 12:50 p.m. on February 27, 2020, Employee #1 was participating in a customer
service skit when she suddenly slumped over in a chair and began to have a
seizure. The employee suffered a subarachnoid hemorrhage medical event and was
hospitalized.
At 8:07 a.m. on December 19, 2019, an employee was working for a wholesaler of
farm and garden machinery and equipment. He maintained machinery. He was working
in the repair shop. He was cutting the top off a 55-gallon (208-liter) 1A1 steel
drum with an oxy-acetylene torch. The drum had contained JD Torq-Gard 30 and
waste 15W-40 engine oil, residual motor oil liquid hydrocarbons that could
produce flammable vapors. The employee had not first removed the 2-in. and
3/4-in. (50-mm and 19-mm) steel bung caps. The drum was therefore completely
enclosed. The heat of the torch ignited the pressurized vapors inside the drum.
The lid roll at the top of the drum release. The drum lid detached from the drum
at high speed and struck the employee in his face and head. He was hospitalized.
The employee suffered the loss of his left eye, several fractures to collarbone,
a broken left elbow, the inability to close his right hand, and several
fractures in his face and eye socket that required a metal plate. There were
unresolved issues regarding his teeth and jaw.
An employee was working at a general medical and surgical hospital. She worked
as an overnight emergency (ER) clerk within the Emergency Department. Her job
responsibilities included performing clerical and receptionist duties for the
Emergency Department. Her job duties included but were not limited to the intake
of emergency room visitors, reviewing and maintenance of patient charts, and
maintenance of the Emergency Department log. On March 25, 2020, she called out
of work sick. On March 30, 2020, she was admitted to a different hospital. On
March 31, 2020, she was transferred from that hospital to the one where she was
employed. On April 1, 2020, she tested positive for COVID-19. At 8:00 a.m. on
April 5, 2020, she died. This was an OSHA-covered fatality.
At 1:30 a.m. on March 19, 2020, an employee was on a work break.  The employee
went to the restroom, and the employee employee passed out in the restroom from
a seizure as attributed to the lack of oxygen.  The cause of the seizure is not
known and may be possibly attributed to the chemical PPA.
At 1:30 p.m. on October 11, 2019, an employee was driving an agricultural
tractor down a farm road and was following three yards behind another tractor
when the front tractor stopped suddenly. The employee was not able to stop on
time and collided with the tractor's attached conveyor belt. The employee was
hospitalized to treat chest and abdominal crushing injuries.
At 12:48 p.m. on December 5, 2019, an employee, a sorter, was pushing empty bins
on a conveyor to be filled with walnuts. Two forklift operators were in the
area, forklift #1 was receiving and moving bins and forklift #2 was filling the
empty bins. Forklift #1 picked up a stack of 4 bins (vertically) and began to
move these bins, while in reverse, near the conveyor. As forklift #1 was
reversing, he started to turn, and the bins became unstable and started to fall.
Forklift #2 then yelled and drove forward in an attempt to prevent the bins from
falling. Forklift #2 was able to block two of the falling bins, but the other
two bins (the top two) continued to fall over the forklift mast and struck the
employee that was pushing the bins on the conveyor. The employee sustained a
head contusion; a fractured vertebra at T-1, T-2, and T-3; a fractured right
finger; a shoulder strain; and internal injuries. She was transported to Modesto
Memorial Medical Center, and admitted for treatment.  The accident occurred at a
nut processing plant. The bins were wood cubes that are approximately 4 feet by
4 feet, and weigh approximately 200-210 pounds each.
At 10:45 p.m. on March 30, 2020, Employee #1, employed by a steel erection
company, and Coworker #1, his supervisor, were engaged in steel erection at a
multiemployer construction project, a new manufacturing structure.  Employee #1
was in the basket of an aerial lift and installing/welding steel cross bars to
an overhead joist.  He became unresponsive, possibly from an electric shock.
The supervisor, using ground controls, proceeded to lower the basket.  When the
basket was approximately 25 feet above the concrete floor, Employee #1 fell
backward from the basket and landed head first.  Emergency services transported
Employee #1 to the hospital, where he was treated for a fractured skull.
Employee #1 died during treatment.
At 10:45 a.m. on April 8, 2020, an employee was working as a machine operator
for a wholesaler of dairy products. English was not her first language. She was
working in the facility's filling room. She was working the PacTec line. A 2008
PacTec model PT-4/6S filling machine, with serial number 2201, was filling
cheese cups with product. During the preceding shift, an issue had arisen with
the machine, in that it was not able to maintain the correct temperature. After
this problem continued, the employee contacted her supervisor and advised him
that the temperature was still too low. The supervisor instructed her to shut
everything off and rinse it. This was the first rinse process of the day. The
employee shut off the cooker so that product would not come into the industrial
stainless steel filler hopper that was part of the PacTec machine. She went to
the control panel and shut everything off and pressed the E-stop button before
starting the rinse process. She then went up onto the platform where the filler
hopper was and grabbed a water hose from the wall and a scrapper. The agitator,
which was located inside of the hopper, was not controlled by the E-stop and
continued to rotate at a slow speed. As the employee cleaned out the hopper, she
was loading equipment onto a cart. The bungee cord attached to the equipment
snapped and hit the employee in the left eye. The employee sustained trauma to
his left eye which required medical treatment without hospitalization. The
employee required his eye be removed at a later date.
At 5:43 p.m. on November 1, 2019, an employee was working for a roofing
contractor that supplies and delivers roofing materials directly to jobsites for
contractors. The employee delivers materials loaded onto a flatbed truck
equipped with an elevating inclined conveyor belt. The employee was assigned to
work with two coworkers to deliver roofing materials to a residential home. The
employee was working on top of the home receiving rolls of roofing material from
the conveyor. The employee had momentarily looked down to put his phone away
with his right hand with his left hand near the conveyor chain. As a result, the
employee caught his left glove in the chain of the conveyor. The conveyor caught
the employee's hand partially pulling off his middle finger. The employee was
treated for a partial amputation to his left middle finger but was not
hospitalized.
At 9:22 p.m. on November 19, 2019, an employee was operating a standup forklift
(Toyota Model: 9BDRU15).  The employee was traveling too fast and placed his
At 7:15 a.m. on September 29, 2019, an employee was walking from an office at an
automotive parts and accessories store.  While walking, the employee tripped
over a tote left on the floor by another manager and fell. The employee
fractured his leg and was hospitalized.
At 6:30 p.m. on October 23, 2019, Employee #1 and Employee #2 were working
customer service and cashiering at a fast food counter. The employees were
attacked by a person who came in off the street. The person chased Employee #1
into the kitchen with gasoline and a lighter and set her on fire. Employee #1
sustained severe burns to her face, chest, neck, shoulders, and extremities and
was hospitalized for treatment. Employee #2 received medical treatment without
requiring hospitalization.
At 1:00 p.m. on November 30, 2019, an employee conducting home care was helping
a resident in and out of a van.  The employee fell in the parking lot and
fractured her right hip.  The employee was hospitalized.
At 11:45 a.m. on October 29, 2019, an employee was installing permanent holiday
lights when he fell from a ladder.  The employee fractured both legs, a wrist,
and sustained a serious head injury and, later, was killed from his injuries.
At 7:45 a.m. on January 29, 2019, an employee was taking part in physical
training inside a gymnasium. He was on the ground attempting to stand up when he
shifted his weight onto his lower right leg. He fractured his leg above the
ankle, requiring hospitalization.
At 12:45 p.m. on October 11, 2019, an employee was operating the Brewer trim saw
to cut boards to length. While cutting, the employee noticed a piece of wood
inside the saw near one of the blades. The employee pressed the stop button and
attempted to pull the piece of wood out of the saw. The saw blades did not
immediately stop turning when the "cycle stop" button was pressed and as the
employee reached into the saw, he contacted one of the blades as it was coasting
to a stop. The employee was hospitalized to treat amputations of his right thumb
and index fingers and lacerations to the three other fingers on his right hand.
At 3:15 p.m. on October 25, 2019, an employee  preparing to weld a perimeter
angle around the top of the structure.  The employee was tied off with a coated
cable anchor strap.  The employee attached a beamer to the top flange of another
beam and detached the coated cable. The employee stepped on a piece of unsecured
bridging and began his fall.  When pressure was applied to the beamer, the
beamer flipped off, causing the employee to fall 18 feet to the ground.  The
employee suffered leg fractures and a concussion, resulting in hospitalization.
At 8:45 p.m. on October 30, 2019, an employee was performing data entry tasks
when he suffered a fatal heart attack or stroke.
At 3:45 p.m. on October 25, 2019, an employee working for a plastic parts
manufactuer was positioning a small trim piece into a notching machine. The
employee had his hand holding the material too close to the point of operation
(die). The employee amputated his left thumb tip and required medical treatment
without hospitalization.
At 1:30 p.m. on October 25, 2019, an employee working for a tire retreading
company was using a 2 by 4 to clear debris from a conveyor belt. The 2 by 4 was
pulled into the machine along with the employee injuring his head, left arm and
shoulder and left hand. The employee amputated his left ring finger and was
hospitalized.
At 8:00 a.m. on October 24, 2019, an employee working as an iron worker for a
structural steel contractor was working from an aerial lift. The employee was
connecting iron when the sleever bar slipped causing the employee to fall
backwards over the guardrail of the lift. The employee fell about 25 feet
breaking multiple bones and requiring hospitalization.
At 1:30 p.m. on October 5, 2019, an employee was removing  finished parts from
the Blaster tumbler with a tote. Employee #1 was removing finished metal parts
by hand when his left hand index finger glove was caught in the tumbler belt and
barrel wheel. Employee #1 received an amputation to his left index finger.  The
employee was hospitalized.
At 9:15 a.m. on October 24, 2019, an employee was standing on the roof of the
maintenance shop inspecting a loose gutter and identifying wires that needed to
be removed. The employee used a Louisville Brute, 6-foot A-frame ladder to climb
onto the air compressor building roof then proceeded to an adjacent roof section
of the maintenance shop. The employee was walking around on top of the
maintenance shop corrugated aluminum roof when he suddenly lost his balance and
slid down the pitched roof and fell 10 to 12 feet to the concrete slab below.
The employee was hospitalized to treat a fractured left elbow and left portion
of the pelvis.
At 01:00 a.m. on June 25, 2019, an employee was serving as a newly assigned
bandsaw operator using an HE&M Twister Automatic Band Saw, Serial Number 794501,
to cut 2-foot lengths of 4-inch by 4-inch rectangular metal tubing. The employee
was in the process of cutting the metal tubing with the bandsaw when the blade
caught the MaxiFlex glove, model number 24-845 CAT II, on the left hand, drawing
it into the blade. The employee sustained an amputation to the left index finger
at the proximal interphalangeal joint which included bone loss. The employee was
treated and released at Sharp Memorial Hospital on June 25, 2019. At 08:15 a.m.
on June 25, 2019, the employer reported the incident incompliance with CSHO
requirements. At 09:10 a.m. on August 23, 2019, CSHO arrived on site to begin
their investigation and a CCR T8 4184(a) citation for not guarding the point of
operation of a machine.
At 6:45 a.m. on October 29,2019, an employee was attempting to remove a board
that had jammed at the entrance of a BREWCO Gang Saw. The employee attempted to
remove the board by jogging the feed controls forward and reverse.  When that
process did not free the board, the employee raised the arbor, bypassing the
machine guard, and reached inside the saw grab the board. The employee performed
this process two more times and on the third attempt to remove the board the
planer head struck his right arm. The employee amputated his arm below the elbow
and was hospitalized.
At 1:15 p.m. on October 28, 2019, an employee was installing roofing and was
moving aluminum pieces across the roof.  When the wind caught the aluminum
of furniture. As the employee pushed the piece of wood through the jointer,
there was resistance causing his hand to slip and make contact with the exposed
portion of the blade. The employee suffered a left middle finger amputation. The
employee was treated but not hospitalized.
At 12:45 p.m. on July 29, 2019, Employee #1, employed by a heating and cooling
company, was working at a residential townhouse.  He was conducting diagnostic
testing on an air conditioning unit when he was electrocuted.  The subsequent
investigation revealed faulty electrical wiring.
At 4:45 p.m. on September 10, 2019, an employee was working outdoors collecting
waste on a residential route when he experienced symptoms of heat illness early
on in the day. At the end of the day, the employee was hospitalized for
treatment of heat exhaustion.
At 10:45 a.m. on August 28, 2019, Employee #1 was spray painting the interior of
a manufacturing plant.  He was adjusting the tip of the sprayer  gun when he
inadvertently pulled the trigger, resulting in a high-pressure injection injury
to his left hand.  The employee required hospitalization for treatment of the
wounded hand.
At 2:00 p.m. on September 14, 2019, an employee was using a DeWalt chipping
hammer to repair foundation at a residential site.  The employee suffered an
electric shock and sustained electrical burns, resulting in hospitalization.
At 9:00 a.m. on August 29, 2019, an employee was setting up the lower die of a
Minster 90-600 Ton Coin Press at a forging facility. The employee was attempting
to remove the lower portion of the die when the machine cycled and caught the
employee's right hand between the bolster and ram. The machine was energized and
no guards were present on the machine at the time of the incident. The employee
was hospitalized to treat an amputation of thumb and index finger and crushing
injuries to the middle, ring and pinky fingers of the right hand.
At 7:30 a.m. on September 11, 2019, an employee was pouring molten aluminum when
he started to feel sick from the heat, but thought he could finish the pour and
continued working. At 2:30 p.m. the employee went to the lunchroom to cool off
but became incoherent. A coworker called an ambulance, and the employee was
hospitalized to treat for heat stress and dehydration.
At 8:15 a.m. on August 26, 2019, an employee had just finished repairing a
grinder and was walking through the wrapping area with the intent to talk to a
coworker. The employee exited the pedestrian-only area through a small gap in a
knee high barrier and approached a stationary forklift from behind (Forklift
#1). The employee was attempting to get to Forklift #2 to talk to a coworker.
Upon getting within arms length of Forklift #1, the forklift started moving
backwards and almost immediately rolled onto the employee's foot. The employee
was hospitalized to treat multiple fractures and breaks in the right foot and
ankle.
At 3:15 p.m. on September 9, 2019, an employee was using an unguarded grinder
with a metal cutting wheel to cut a piece of metal.  The grinder got bound up
and kicked back, striking the employee's leg.  The employee was hospitalized for
treatment of  deep laceration.
At 1:30 p.m. on April 8, 2019, an employee was cutting pieces of wood on a miter
saw when the saw kicked back and his gloved left hand was caught by the blade.
was caught and forced upwards crushing it between the half inch gap between the
rotating metal paddles and the frame of the machine. The employee fractures his
arm, which was amputated midway, and required hospitalization.
At 11:45 a.m. on September 26, 2019, an employee was operating a blanking press
and feeder. The employee attempted to unjam a part caught in the die while the
machine was operating. There was no guard in place where parts came out of the
press to prevent employee from reaching the point of operation. The employee
amputated his right pinky finger and was hospitalized.
At 2:30 p.m. on October 15, 2019, an employee was attempting to reposition a
34.5 inch by 96 inch 836 grade steel heat shield on a shop-made furnace. The
heat shield was attached to a set of brackets attached to a gas powered furnace.
When the employee pulled the shield forward, the part slipped off of the
brackets and fell. The employee caught his left index finger in between the
falling heat shield and the 2-inch diameter bar rest. The employee amputated his
finger above the second knuckle and was hospitalized.
At 3:45 p.m. on October 12, 2019, an employee was operating a meat grinder and
was trying to clean out the shaft on the bone collector. The bone collector
contained bone and fat not wanted in the final product. Inside the shaft was a
moving piston that moved from left to right. The bone collector was designed to
push unwanted bones and fat that dropped down inside a tube and into a garbage

On December 23, 2019, an employee was working as a laborer for a wholesale
grocery supply firm. He was working at a shipping and receiving warehouse
operated by the firm. He was working as a pallet sorter. He was working on the
salvage dock at the warehouse. At the salvage dock in the warehouse, employees

logistics. This practice had existed for years,l but there were typically not
too many bales on the dock and plenty of space. There was a designated area, a
standardized practice, and a method for stacking bales. The day of the incident

were stacked four high. This was a normal height, but because one or more bales

feet (2.9 to 3.1 meters). Each bale weighed about 300 pounds (140 kg). A stack

stacks unstable without pallets. Add in the issue of damaged bales at the
bottom, and this method of stacking was unsecure. In this incident, the employee
was operating a pallet jack. As he was moving pallets near a stack, the top one
or two bales fell off and struck him in his back and in the back of his head. He
was taken by ambulance to a hospital and admitted with back and head injuries.
He was hospitalized for two or more days. The firm's management team was aware
of the hazard. All the managers typically walked through this area and had seen
the process. The shift supervisor also knew about the stacking process and the
method of stacking bales. The employee was not reprimanded.
